item.title: Native Influences on America
item.description:
Spirituality

Native Influences on America

How Native American cultures helped to form modern America.

Posted July 2, 2026

Key points
  • The American Constitution’s concept of a nonhierarchical society was inspired by Native American cultures.
  • The idea of a union of different states was adopted from the Native Nations League of the Iroquois.
  • Indigenous principles are also reflected strongly in modern environmental and spiritual philosophies.
Governor William Burnet of New York meets with Native American leaders in 1721
Source: Wikimedia Commons, public domain

On the 250th anniversary of American independence, it’s important to remember and respect the cultures that flourished on the American continent long before European colonists arrived, and that were tragically decimated and disrupted by the colonists.

Nobody knows for sure how many indigenous people inhabited the American continent before Columbus’ arrival in 1492. Estimates range from 45 million to 100 million, and the real figure probably lies midway between. But after European contact, the figure declined rapidly, mainly due to the spread of disease and the loss of food sources (both of which were sometimes intentional, such as when colonists killed buffalo and burned crops, or gave the Indians infected blankets and food). By 1860, there were only 340,000 Indians left in North America. The 1920 U.S. Census Bureau counted 244,437 Native Americans. Fortunately, the figure has increased since then, and now around 9.7 million Americans identify as solely or partly Native American.

One aspect of American history that often isn’t emphasized is the extent to which European colonists were influenced by the ideals and customs of indigenous Americans. The American Constitution’s essential concept of a non-hierarchical society in which everybody had equal rights was largely inspired—both indirectly and directly—by Native American societies.

The Influence of Native Americans on Early American Ideals

The indirect influence was through the French philosopher Jean-Jacques Rousseau. In Europe, it had always been taken for granted that some human beings were born superior to others and entitled to special rights and privileges. The first powerful statement of the idea that human beings were born equal was Rousseau’s The Social Contract, published in 1762. Rousseau was heavily influenced by the accounts he had read of early European people’s encounters with indigenous peoples of the Americas and the South Pacific. The Social Contract influenced the founding fathers of America.

At the same time, more significantly, the founding fathers were influenced by their own observations of what Rousseau called the "natural liberty" and egalitarianism of Native American societies. As the anthropologist Alvin Josephy wrote of the Hopi Indians, for example, “In none of the towns were there social classes or differences in wealth; everyone, even members of the theocracies, worked and shared as equals.”1 Both Thomas Jefferson and Benjamin Franklin wrote in their memoirs that they were influenced by the Iroquois model of democratic government, with its system of checks and balances and elected representatives.

article continues after advertisement

In addition, the idea of a union of different states was adopted from the Native Nations League of the Iroquois (the Haudenosaunee)—in fact, the idea was recommended to the Europeans by a leader of the Six Nations at a treaty signing in 1744, at which Benjamin Franklin was present. The League had its own carefully worked out constitution and laws, which leaders learned by heart and passed on orally from generation to generation, and the founding fathers borrowed liberally from all of them. In I751, Franklin printed out an account of an Iroquois council meeting to use as a model, believing that if native tribes could form a lasting peaceful union, then the colonies could too. (Although, as the Native American and Mestiza scholar M.A. Jaimes Guerrero has pointed out, the one important part the founding fathers omitted was the authority and leadership of the clan mothers.2)

Environmental and Spiritual Philosophies

There are other more subtle ways in which the principles of Native American cultures have manifested themselves. Two of the most significant cultural developments over the last few decades have been the ecological and spiritual movements. It’s difficult to say whether these have been directly influenced by Native American—or other indigenous—cultures, but there are certainly strong parallels.

Indigenous attitudes toward nature are characterized by what anthropologists call a "kincentric ecology."3 This is why it’s common to use familial terms—like sister, brother, mother, or grandmother—to refer to animals and plants or the Earth itself. The Lakota use the phrase mitakuye oyasin—which translates as "all my relations"—to express their kinship with all natural phenomena. As summarized by the Lakota leader Chief Luther Standing Bear, for his people, "Kinship with all creatures of the earth, soil and water was a real and active principle."4 This attitude encourages a sense of respect and responsibility for the natural world, which is the essence of modern environmental philosophy.

On a spiritual level, the most significant aspect of Native American cultures is the concept of an all-pervading spiritual energy or force. The Hopi referred to this as maasauu; the Lakota called it wakan-tanka (often translated as Great Spirit, or Great Mystery). In the Northeastern woodlands, the Haudenosaunee called it orenda, while Algonquian groups called it manitou, and so on. A member of the Pawnee tribe—who referred to spirit-force as tirawa—described it poetically as a force which "is in everything and…moves upon the darkness, the night, and causes her to bring forth the dawn. It is the breath of the new-born dawn."5

article continues after advertisement

As well as pervading all natural phenomena, this spiritual force or energy is seen as the essence of human beings, too, so that we are essentially one with all phenomena. At the same time, there is often an inference that the force is beyond the world, that it is both immanent and transcendent. The sense of oneness with all phenomena, and the awareness of a spiritual quality within us, are the essence of spiritual experience, and the principles of every spiritual tradition.

In this way, Native American cultures are imbued with spiritual, environmental, and democratic principles, which now permeate modern American culture (and many other cultures around the world). On July 4th, and on any day, these influences should be acknowledged with respect and gratitude.

item.title: The Paradox of Taking Breaks
item.description:
Executive Function

The Paradox of Taking Breaks

Why and how to take frictionless breaks.

Posted July 2, 2026

Key points
  • Breaks help refresh your brain and body but can add tough transitions to your day.
  • You do not have to earn a break, but taking one may increase your productivity.
  • You can set yourself up for better transitions coming back from a break.

“I just feel so overwhelmed,” I sigh as I hit the couch. It’s been a long day, and I still have dinner to make, an attempt at a workout, and a cat to medicate before bed. The inner pull to sink into the couch and rest is countered by an anxious energy that says I must keep pushing forward. Fearing I might fall asleep or lose momentum if I rest “too long,” I start to stand again.

“That’s it?” my husband asks, and pats the seat next to him. “It’s OK to take a break,” he says, as he pulls up a gym fail video—a surefire way to get my attention. My internal parts are at odds—wanting to relax and wanting to finish the to-do list for the day—and now they’re mixing with a part that doesn’t want to disappoint my sweet husband.

“One video,” I agree, knowing it will likely be three. After a while, I’ve settled into the rhythm of making dinner, which doesn’t feel so arduous after a little rest. My husband’s just come inside from putting the chickens away for the night, and he jokes that he thinks I’m allergic to rest. He might be right.

Why We Resist Taking Breaks

Why is it that we resist taking a break? And are there ways to make breaks a frictionless part of our days?

Most of the amazing humans I coach also have a complicated interaction with breaks. They can recognize the visceral, positive changes in their bodies and moods after taking a break, but the act of convincing themselves to take said break can end up feeling like another task. The transition between work and break can be tricky to navigate, but it’s nothing compared to the transition back to work after a break. (Think about the awful nightly migration you have to do from watching your favorite shows to brushing your teeth and getting ready for bed. It feels impossible, and it’s a perfect example of the fun-to-work transition.) Many people dread the transition back into work and will avoid breaks because they don’t trust themselves to come back.

Breaks can feel complicated for brains with executive dysfunction
Source: Tara Winstead / Pexels

Another roadblock for taking a break is the belief we have to “earn” it. This line of thinking says we must be productive enough to pause and rest, delaying movement, enjoyment, even using the bathroom or having a snack until we’ve accomplished a task. The major flaw in this approach is that taking breaks can increase productivity; the task we force ourselves to complete so we “earn” our break may take 20 minutes with a tired brain but only 5 after refreshing for a few minutes. Productivity aside, humans are mammals, and the idea that we have to complete tasks in order to rest reflects a social construct, one that is not rooted in biology.

Strategies for Making Breaks Easier and More Effective

There are several ways to honor your need for a break without having the break derail your day. One powerful way is to schedule them; give yourself transition periods that include an activity that gives you what you need, and honor that schedule. If you struggle with time blindness, consider using a visual timer or alarms to help you come back to your task—it could even be several alarms to give you a heads-up that the break is almost up.

article continues after advertisement

Another idea is to have several breaks in mind, so you have a variety of options depending on what you need and how distractible you feel. For example, on a day when it’s been really tricky to focus, I may choose a break that is rewarding but won’t glue my attention for hours: a quick bit of yoga or walking to the mailbox (it’s .2 miles round trip) may help me feel more energized but won’t suck me in like a show might. On the other hand, if I really need a good break, I may call a friend or walk the neighborhood, activities that can extend for a while when I have the flexibility.

To help Future You with the transition back into work mode, leave everything set up when you take your break. Not having to sign in or set up again removes potential friction. You can add social accountability by telling a coworker or friend when you’ll be back from your break, too. When the transition is particularly tough, consider asking your brain to just do “5 awful minutes” of the task. Often you will find that you will hit your rhythm again and be empowered to stay for much longer than the 5 minutes.

Breaks can evoke a lot of feelings and have loads of societal stories about them. Listen to your body and honor what you need. You can borrow ideas to make breaks easier to take and return from, too.

item.title: Dreaming With the Founding Fathers
item.description:
Dreaming

Dreaming With the Founding Fathers

The dream-sharing of Benjamin Rush and John Adams took an eerie prophetic turn.

Posted July 2, 2026

Key points
  • Two early leaders of the American Revolution agreed to share their dreams as a friendly pastime.
  • Their dreams gave them both personal and political/historical insights.
  • The dream-sharing process prepared the way for a crucial reconciling.
Source: Kelly Bulkeley

This Fourth of July not only marks America’s 250th birthday. It also represents the 200th anniversary of the deaths of country’s second and third presidents, John Adams and Thomas Jefferson, who passed away within five hours of each other on July 4, 1826.

More remarkable than the patriotic timing of their deaths is the fact that several years earlier Dr. Benjamin Rush, a mutual friend and signer of the Declaration of Independence, foresaw their simultaneous deaths in a dream.

Despite both serving as visionary leaders during the early, perilous days of the country, Adams and Jefferson became political enemies with drastically differing ideas about America’s future and how to get there. This caused distress for other revolutionary figures like Rush who feared their titanic disagreements would be too much for the fragile nation to endure.

Rush took it upon himself in 1805 to engage with Adams, initiating a regular correspondence with him, and nudging him toward an eventual reconciliation with Jefferson. To accomplish this delicate diplomatic mission, Rush used a surprising method: He suggested to Adams that, instead of discussing common issues of the day in their letters, they share their dreams with each other.

As Joseph Ellis recounts in his Pulitzer-Prize winning book Founding Brothers (2002), “Adams leapt at the suggestion and declared himself prepared to match his old friend ‘dream for dream.’”

There followed a remarkable exchange of dreams, interpretations, and insights both personal and political. Rush, a physician acting as a kind of proto-psychoanalyst, slowly but surely brought Adams around to a more charitable and balanced view of Jefferson. Then, in 1809, Rush reported to Adams “his most amazing dream yet”:

He dreamed that Adams had written a short letter to Jefferson, congratulating him on his recent retirement from public life. Jefferson had then responded to this magnanimous gesture with equivalent graciousness… Then the two philosopher-kings ‘sunk into the grave nearly at the same time, full of years and rich in the gratitude and praises of their country.’

According to Ellis, Adams sent Rush an immediate and enthusiastic response: “‘A DREAM AGAIN! I have no other objection to your dream but that it is not history. It may be prophecy.’”

At this time, Adams and Jefferson were still estranged; they did not resume their friendship until 1812. Rush’s dream thus predates their reconciliation by three years and their “nearly at the same time” deaths by 17 years. To anticipate the former in a dream is impressive; to anticipate the latter in a dream is uncanny.

article continues after advertisement

However, not even Rush’s evidently fertile prophetic imagination could foresee the poetic wonder of these two American giants entering the grave together on the Fourth of July, 1826, 50 years after the signing of the country’s founding document.

Other than adding a kind of mystical halo to early American history, what can we today learn from this remarkable process of dream-sharing among the Founding Fathers? For one thing, it sounds like they were having fun. The dreams they described to each other are as wild and bizarre as anyone else’s, and both Rush and Adams clearly enjoyed devoting their formidable mental powers to analyzing the curious meanings of each other’s oneiric experiences.

It also sounds like their dream-sharing provided them with a genuinely new understanding of recent political history and their roles in it. In addition to making valuable discoveries about their personal lives, Rush and Adams found their dreams led them to a deeper appreciation for the psycho-spiritual significance of the epic events they had helped to bring into being.

Perhaps of greatest relevance for our concerns two centuries later, a practical outcome of their process was the healing of a bitter political division: E pluribus unum, with an assist from dreaming. This was Rush’s initial goal, and he achieved it spectacularly. Of course, the reconciliation didn’t happen overnight; it took several years of patient dream-sharing to get there. But once resumed, the Adams-Jefferson friendship remained strong and respectful until their symbolically appropriate end. On the bicentennial of their deaths, it seems fitting to highlight their admirable, dream-mediated willingness to set aside their political conflicts and find common ground in supporting and celebrating the highest ideals of our nation.

item.title: How Leisure Activities Can Promote You Professionally
item.description:
Career

How Leisure Activities Can Promote You Professionally

Personal life choices convey competence and credibility.

Posted July 2, 2026

Key points
  • Disclosing leisure activities enhanced perceptions of professional competence.
  • Employers and consumers are positively influenced by personal pursuits.
  • Activities such as cooking and hiking are viewed more positively than watching television.
Source: Michael Silfverskiöld / Pixabay

In a competitive economy, consumers and potential employers are faced with a variety of choices. When selecting a product, service, or potential new employee, they look for more than experience; they also value credibility and competence. In perceiving these traits, all of us consider more than credentials; we are influenced by someone’s leisure activities and hobbies as well. Research explains.

Reading Beyond the Resume

Michelle E. Daniels et al. (2025) investigated the value of accessing and evaluating holistic information about service providers in a piece entitled “What Do You Do Outside of Work?”[i] They found that disclosing leisure activities enhanced perceptions of competence, positively impacting potential consumers.

Daniels et al. begin by recognizing that consumers today have access to more holistic and inclusive information about providers they are considering hiring or working with, such as designers and realtors. This information includes not only a professional portfolio, but also how providers spend their free time. Daniels et al. note that while some might think leisure time activities are unrelated to professional ability, they actually found that disclosing leisure activities was linked with “eudaimonic” well-being, manifest as experiencing fulfillment or finding meaning. They cite cooking and hiking as examples of activities that can have a positive impact on consumer choice.

Daniels et al. also found that leisure time disclosures, when compared to not disclosing or disclosing less eudaimonic activities such as relaxing or watching television, result in higher perceptions of competence, leading to a greater willingness to support and employ such individuals.

The Professional Allure of Personal Leisure

Daniels et al. demonstrated through five studies that what some people might consider irrelevant personal information about professional providers can actually positively impact consumer choice. Their research included specific examples.

In an advertising context, they found that consumers were more likely to click on an ad showcasing a service provider describing her eudaimonic leisure activities than an ad without that type of information. Dealing with students, they found that consumers demonstrated a greater willingness to support the professional pursuits of students who disclosed eudaimonic leisure preferences, compared to students who disclosed less or no eudaimonic leisure.

article continues after advertisement

Daniels et al. also found that consumers who expected to rely on someone else were more likely to choose to work with individuals who disclosed more rather than less eudaimonic leisure—a choice that was mediated by competence. In their final two studies they showed that the link between eudaimonic leisure and consumer choice is mainly driven by perceptions of competence, rather than authentic, openness, warmth, or what they describe as cultural capital.

Balancing Professional With Personal

In one of the most impactful parts of their research, Daniels et al. describe the people who are in a position to benefit most from their research: people just beginning their professional lives or changing careers—transitioning to an area where they lack essential indicators of competence. In these situations, they suggest that simple strategies such as disclosing eudaimonic leisure activities may help individuals with limited experience distinguish themselves from the pack of other job candidates.

Apparently, successful marketing appears to involve showcasing positive personal pursuits in a fashion that will capture the interest of consumers and employers. Whether connecting through curiosity or capitalizing on common ground, individuals benefit from sharing information about themselves both professionally and personally.
